body.text: Concern 'big money' is flowing into Victoria's election despite donation cap
In short:
Tens of thousands of dollars in political donations spread across linked companies have raised concerns about a "loophole" in Victoria's donor laws.
In one case, 20 entities linked to two individuals donated $98,000 — well above the limit of $5,030 for individuals at the time.
Transparency International says the legally valid donations constitute a "loophole" that goes against the intention of the state's donation laws.

Tens of thousands of dollars in election donations from companies linked to property developers, the construction and investment advisory industries have flowed to a Victorian political party, despite a new cap aimed at keeping "big money out of elections".

Victoria brought in a cap on what any one person or "related bodies corporate" could donate to a single political party or independent candidate earlier this year, with then-premier Jacinta Allan pledging "Victoria's elections should be decided by Victorians — not by who has the deepest pockets".

The new law capped donations at $5,030 between April 15 and and June 30, then rising to $5,190 until November 28 — the day of the election. After this, the cap rises to around $7,500 over the following four years, accounting for indexation.

Analysis by the ABC has found donations from linked companies totalling well above the relevant period's cap, including one case where 20 entities linked to two property developers donated $98,000 in one week.
The transactions appear to comply with the new rules because they do not meet the strict definition of "related bodies corporate" in the Corporations Act.

Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the rules created a "loophole … [that] clearly goes against the intention of the reforms" and that large donations risked eroding public trust in democracy.
"We're seeing in Victoria and other states trust in our democracy and political parties at all-time lows," Mr Moore said.

"Voters see property developers, data centre companies, rich individuals donate thousands of dollars to candidates and political parties … there's a perception that these entities are getting a quid pro quo, and you know, potentially getting something in return for their donations."
Ex-footballer turned developer kicks in $20,000

In one case in late August, three companies wholly-owned and directed by former AFL star-turned major property development player Fraser Brown donated $5,000 each, totalling $15,000, to the Victorian branch of the Liberal Party.
The companies, called GPH No.1, GPH No.4 and GPH Plant, are all registered at the same address as Brown Property Group in Hawthorn.
Mr Brown also donated $5,000 in his own name on that same day, as did two family members.
Brown Property has in recent years snapped up tightly contested land across the city, reportedly paying $250 million last year for a kale farm in Clyde North.
The group lists eight active house and land planned communities with a self-assessed development value of at least $1.7 billion.
Mr Brown did not respond to the ABC's requests for comment.

In a separate case in early September, five firms linked to two directors of a major construction services company, Checkpoint, each made a donation of $5,000 to the Victorian Liberal Party, totalling $25,000.

Four of the companies, which all include the term "CBS" in the title, are jointly majority owned, via another company, by Checkpoint directors Gavin Casey and Clement Giambattista, while the fifth is majority owned by companies of which they are directors.
Mr Giambattista and Mr Casey did not respond to the ABC's requests for comment.

In another case in mid-May, three companies — Ketom 2, Ketom 3 and Ketom Pty Ltd — jointly owned by investment advisory specialist Ronn Bechler and Maxine Bechler, made three donations of $5,000 each to the Victorian Liberal Party.
Mr Bechler told the ABC he did not wish to discuss political donations.
Developers pledge almost $100,000 in one week
Meanwhile it's emerged donations by a group of companies linked to three other wealthy property developers were far higher than initially reported in the media.

The Age in September reported that between late April and early May a dozen businesses with variations on the name "Mensch", made a total of $58,800 donations to the Victorian arm of the Liberal Party.
Three men were linked to all firms either via shareholdings or directorships.

They were David Scalzo, the scion of a food import and distribution empire, Califam Constructions managing director Anthony Caligiuri and Eli Goldfinger, who runs a corporate advisory consultancy specialising in property development, compliance and succession planning.
Analysis by the ABC has revealed the total figure of donations linked to two of these men — Mr Caligiuri and Mr Goldfinger — is in fact higher.
A further eight firms of which Mr Goldfinger and Mr Caliguiri are directors also made donations over the same period of $4,900 each.
In total, the ABC has identified 20 firms with links to Mr Goldfinger and Mr Caliguiri which donated a total of $98,000 over a one-week period to the Liberal Party's Victorian branch.
A spokesman for this group of 20 entities, which includes Mensch Investments, thanked the ABC for acknowledging that separate company donations were lawful.
He said each company acted with integrity and full disclosure.
"Each donation was reported to the Victorian Electoral Commission in the manner prescribed by the VEC on its website, subjecting each donation to VEC vetting," the spokesman said.
"We encourage anyone else wishing to exercise their democratic right of donating to also act lawfully and to disclose and report donations to the VEC.
"We assume the government has thoughtfully designed donation laws, especially after having the advantage of High Court scrutiny of donation laws earlier this year.
"Over many years we have supported productive and visionary members of parliament across the political spectrum at both a state and federal level."
The Victorian Electoral Commission said it did not comment on specific cases.
It said related bodies corporate were defined as when one company was a holding company of the other, one is a subsidiary of the other, or one is a subsidiary of a holding company of the other.
"Common ownership by a single individual does not mean, by itself, that companies are related bodies corporate," the spokesperson said.
"We expect parties and other donation recipients to have processes and procedures in place to identify donations made or received from related entities."
Laws changed in wake of High Court ruling
Victoria's donation laws were overhauled after a High Court decision handed down on April 15 struck out an entire section of the existing Act dealing with caps on political donations.

The existing laws were challenged by two independent candidates — Paul Hopper and Melissa Lowe — who argued the donations cap was unfair and risked allowing established political parties to benefit from wealthy donors where new and independent candidates could not.
The High Court decision left the state without any regulation of political donations in the lead-up to the November poll.
Victoria's parliament then scrambled to pass new laws in June that restored caps on donations and reinstated public disclosure requirements and public funding.
The new legislation was applied retrospectively to any donations received between April 15 and November 28, where any donations received above the $5,190 cap were to be returned to donors.

The ABC asked the Victorian Liberal Party, which were the recipients of all four cases identified, whether they had examined any of those transactions, or returned any donations from any source after the new laws were introduced.
A Victorian Liberal Party spokesperson replied that "the Liberal Party operates in compliance with the requirements of the Electoral Act".

Companies are not required to publicly reveal their ownership or directorship structure when disclosing donations, which means the ABC cannot say whether there are more examples of these kinds of companies making donations across the political spectrum.
Transparency International Australia's Clancy Moore said the ABC's investigation showed the need for greater beneficial ownership transparency.
Victoria's new laws have an in-built review by an expert panel, which will form after the election and hand down its findings late next year.
Mr Moore said he hoped the review would look at the "loophole" present in the laws, which he said were rushed through parliament without proper scrutiny.
"Because it's really not the intent of the government's law to have corporate entities donating up to $100,000 in the lead up to an election," Mr Moore said.
He also urged the panel to consider banning donations from "high risk" industries, such as property developers.

"It's particularly risky, there's clearly a risk of poor governance and even a risk of corruption when you have private interests involved in planning, in construction, in those economic sectors that are regulated by government but also have key decisions like an approval process or a tendering process, where you have those entities donating large amounts of money, because it could either knowingly or unknowingly influence government decision-makers," Mr Moore said.
"It absolutely feeds into a perception of the system being rigged, and, you know, governments favouring private interests against the interests of citizens."
